title: Pacific Pulse
pitch: A record-chasing El Nino is warming the tropical Pacific this autumn, and how strong it looks depends on the ruler used to measure it. The visitor flips between four rulers (classic ONI, NOAA's new relative index, monthly and daily Nino 3.4), watches the all-time table of events re-sort around a 2026 marker, and sets what-if peaks to see which records fall on which ruler. A bet card scores a guess against history and the forecasters, and a WebAudio drone follows the heat, so the page doubles as a small lesson in how a 'strongest ever' headline gets made.
whyNow: NOAA's 2026-10-08 update keeps an El Nino Advisory in effect with the event still strengthening, late-September daily readings of Nino 3.4 passed +3 C, and forecasters centre the peak near +3.6 to +3.7 C. NOAA now also reports a relative index (RONI), so 'strongest ever' is a live argument about measurement. Numbers move with each monthly update, so every value on the page is stamped with its s...

research.summary: An El Nino is strengthening in the tropical Pacific and is on course to challenge the records. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center update of 2026-10-08 keeps the El Nino Advisory in effect and calls the event still strengthening; Carbon Brief and IRI put Nino 3.4 near +3 C by late September, and forecasters centre the peak around +3.6 to +3.7 C. The yardstick is contested: classic ONI peaks are about 2.6 (2015-16), 2.3 to 2.4 (1997-98) and 2.2 (1982-83), a monthly Nino 3.4 series ranks 1982-83 above 1997-98, and NOAA now also reports a relative index (RONI) that removes tropical-mean warming. That measurement argument plus a short, dated list of numbers per ruler is small enough to bundle by hand and gives the page its story.

facts.claim: On 2026-10-08 NOAA's Climate Prediction Center kept an El Nino Advisory in effect and described the event as still strengthening; a ski-weather outlet's October-update headline also reports a strengthening event.

RONI is the 3-month Nino 3.4 anomaly minus the tropical-mean SST anomaly (20N-20S), rescaled to the variance of the classic ONI, on a 1991-2020 base; NOAA says past episodes will be re-evaluated, so classifications can differ from ONI.

title: Extra Attacker
pitch: A late-game coaching trainer built on a real solver: each round deals a clock, a goal margin and a faceoff, the visitor chooses when to pull the goalie, and a backward-induction model grades the call in expected standings points using published scoring rates. A policy map shows where the math says to pull for every deficit, overlaid with the league-average pull time that has drifted earlier since 2013-14, while a crowd soundscape turns a backfired pull into a hush with a lone cricket in it. It arrives days after a goalie scored into an empty net.
whyNow: Early in the 2026-27 NHL season a Rangers goalie scored into an empty net on 2026-10-01, reported as the 18th goalie ever to do so, which puts late-game empty nets in the headlines. The underlying question, when to pull the goalie, is evergreen: it arises in every close game, and the league-wide timing has drifted earlier for a decade.

research.summary: Pulling the goalie is one of hockey's few decisions that can be settled with arithmetic, and it has a literature (operations-research papers, a 2018 study on 2015-16 NHL data, club analytics columns). The models disagree on the optimum, and one analysis found in search results argues realised benefits are smaller than simulations imply. Coach behaviour has moved: an NHL.com club column puts the average time left at a one-goal pull at about 73 s in 2013-14 and about 97 s in 2020-21 (peak about 106 s in 2019-20), and another outlet also reports coaches pulling earlier than ever. The hook is confirmed by three independent outlets: on 2026-10-01 a Rangers goalie scored into an empty net after Tampa Bay pulled its own, the 18th goalie in NHL history to score. The rate parameters come from single summaries and stay flagged; the page treats them as adjustable presets.

title: Pick Autopsy
pitch: A visitor drafts a deck of about ten cards for a tiny invented deckbuilder, choosing, skipping or trimming at four forks, and a worker then plays that deck ten thousand seeded runs, painting a 100-by-100 field of wins and losses in a blink. The autopsy replays every fork both ways and splits the win-rate change fairly across the four choices, so the visitor sees which pick carried the run, which was a decoy and which quietly cost points, each with an honest error bar. Ranking the forks before the reveal earns an intuition grade, and any pixel replays its run card by card.
whyNow: Timeless. Deckbuilder folklore (skip rewards, thin the deck, trust the combo) tends to be argued from the runs a player happens to remember, and this page measures it for one invented game with ten thousand runs per fork. Genre backdrop, reported and unconfirmed: Slay the Spire 2 has been in Early Access since 2026-03-05 per the studio's news post.

research.summary: Fan guides for Slay the Spire treat skipping card rewards and trimming starter Strikes and Defends as a deliberate way to keep a deck thin (one guide suggests staying under about 15 cards unless the deck leans on card draw); guides and forums reportedly disagree on the right size, per a blended search summary, so that point is shown as reported. Opening-hand and draw odds follow the hypergeometric distribution (several trading-card math pages). Deck testers say comparing win rates by hand needs far more games than people play. Methods: the Shapley value averages a choice's marginal contribution over all orderings and the parts sum exactly to the total, which for four forks needs only 16 deck variants; common random numbers are the textbook way to compare simulations. Derived by the scout in a throwaway seeded Node prototype of an invented game, not from the web: 10,000 runs took about 0.13 s, a 16-variant batch 2 to 3.5 s, Shapley parts summed to the total in 8 of 8 scenarios, and matched seeds cut variance only 2 to 24 percent for single-card swaps, so accuracy rests on run count.

title: Shuffle Sharp
pitch: A lazy dealer riffles a fresh 52-card deck once or twice and a visitor, playing the sharp, calls each next card as it turns over. After a single idealised riffle about 31 cards can be called against 4.5 for blind guessing (the scout's seeded count), and each extra shuffle melts that edge until it is near half a card at seven riffles. A feint mode adds false shuffles and perfect faros that only look mixed, and an exact curve shows why seven is the magic number.
whyNow: Timeless. A famous result becomes something felt in the fingers: exploiting a lazy shuffle is the card-table version of exploiting a strategy that mixes too little, and the curve is the plain-language picture of unexploitable play. In board-game deckbuilders every reshuffle of a hand-shuffled discard pile is a place where order can leak.

research.summary: After k riffles a deck holds only arrangements with at most 2^k rising sequences, and the chance of an arrangement depends only on its rising-sequence count r as C(2^k + n - r, n) over 2^(kn); the scout checked this law by exhaustive enumeration for small decks. Exact 52-card total variation distance (computed by the scout from Eulerian numbers) is 1.000 through k=4, then 0.924, 0.614, 0.334, 0.167, 0.085, 0.043 for k=5 to 10, matching the often-cited rule of about seven riffles (Harvey Mudd, MathWorks, Science News, the Bayer-Diaconis paper). title: The Gas Remembers
pitch: A visitor types a word and about 1,500 coloured particles spell it out; a gas simulation then scatters it into confetti while an entropy meter climbs. Pressing rewind runs the same laws backwards and the word re-forms, sealed by a bit-for-bit return receipt, because integer arithmetic makes every step exactly undoable. Switching to ordinary floating point, or nudging one particle by one part in a million, breaks the return, and a V-shaped mismatch curve points to the moment and the particle of the nudge.
whyNow: Timeless. The arrow-of-time puzzle is about 150 years old, yet a toy that lets anyone break the reversal by hand is rare, and clips of dye unmixing in glycerin keep circulating (one was fact-checked as authentic).

research.summary: Time-symmetric dynamics would retrace their path when every velocity is flipped; Loschmidt raised this against Boltzmann's H-theorem and Boltzmann answered that reversed states exist but are overwhelmingly rare. Floating-point simulations rarely manage it: the forward-and-back error grows exponentially in chaotic systems. Levesque and Verlet (1993) described an integer-arithmetic scheme that is exactly reversible, and later bit-reversible integrators use the same idea. University demos of dye unmixing in glycerin show the physical cousin. Scout prototype, not literature: 400 soft disks on a 2^20 integer lattice with antisymmetric rounded pair forces returned bit-exactly after 1500 steps out and 1500 back; a one-unit nudge grew by a factor e every 8 to 27 steps depending on density, and the mismatch against the clean replay had its apex at the nudge step. Model limits: 2D soft disks, a small gas, coarse-grained entropy, no quantum effects; Lyapunov rates are measured in the page and depend on its parameters.

design.coreLoop: The visitor chooses a word, lets the gas disperse it, rewinds time and reads the return receipt, which compares the final state with the start bit for bit. The physical analogue (dye in glycerol) fails once diffusion intervenes, so the page states what is modelled (exact arithmetic) and what is not, and does not suggest that real gases un-mix.

title: The Shortcut Trap
pitch: A weight hangs from two springs and a few strings, and a visitor predicts whether snipping the short linking string will drop or lift it; the weight rises, against intuition. Sliders for string length and spring stiffness reveal the narrow band where this happens, a bounce metronome shows the weight vibrating twice as fast after the cut, and a mapping toggle recasts the same network as roads where closing a free shortcut cuts everyone's commute from 80 to 65 minutes in the textbook case. A puzzle mode deals random networks with a cut budget and scores the lift against the best possible.
whyNow: Timeless. Road-closure and induced-demand arguments keep returning, and the spring version of the Braess paradox keeps resurfacing in physics lecture demos and blogs (posts from 2025 and 2026 turned up in search).

research.summary: In 1991 Cohen and Horowitz published a string-and-spring network in which cutting a string that supports a weight makes the weight rise, with an electrical analogue and a traffic analogy; it is formally the Braess paradox (1968), where adding a free road raises every driver's travel time. With the linking string intact the two springs act in series (k/2) while two longer safety strings hang slack; after the cut the safety strings take over and the springs act in parallel (2k), so the weight sits higher by W/(2k) minus an offset (read by the scout as the slack left in the safety strings). Scout check, not literature: a small static solver for equal springs, load F, stiffness k gave a lift that peaks at F/(2k), is positive only inside a band of safety-string lengths of width F/k, and is negative above it. Textbook traffic version: 4000 drivers, 65 minutes becoming 80 after a free link. Model limits: ideal massless springs, inextensible strings, quasi-static equilibrium, linear latencies, selfish routing; the paradox needs those conditions and the page says so.

facts.claim: Cohen and Horowitz (Nature 352, 699-701, 22 August 1991) described a string-and-spring network in which cutting a string that supports a weight makes the weight rise at equilibrium, with an electrical analogue and a traffic analogy.

With the linking string intact the two springs act in series (effective stiffness k/2) and the secondary strings hang slack; after the cut the secondary strings take the load and the springs act in parallel (2k, four times stiffer), so each spring carries half the weight and the weight sits higher.

The net rise is W/(2k) minus the original stretch, so the effect exists only when that stretch is smaller than W/(2k); a small amount of slack in the strings cannot make up for the reduced spring extension, so the mass ends up higher.

University lecture-demo collections list the demonstration: a catalogue entry named Spring and String Thing (B4-04) described as a counterintuitive series-and-parallel demo, and a demo page titled Spring Paradox (B17).

In the textbook Braess network (credited to Dietrich Braess, 1968), 4000 drivers choose between two routes, each a leg taking T/100 minutes (T = drivers on it) plus a fixed 45-minute leg; an even split takes 65 minutes, while a free link between the midpoints sends everyone over both congestible legs for 80 minutes and no one gains by switching back.

Reported, not confirmed: commonly cited real-world cases are Stuttgart (1969, a new downtown street worsened congestion and was closed), Seoul (Cheonggyecheon expressway removal, about 2003-2005) and New York (42nd Street closed for Earth Day 1990 without the predicted gridlock); sources differ on details.
Reported, not confirmed: lecture slides state that the paradox arises under selfish (user-optimal) routing and does not arise when a planner assigns system-optimal routes.

title: Forty Steps To Lunch
pitch: A visitor enters their lunch options and a few moods, then watches the candidates roll down a forty-station contraption where every station runs a real decision method: budget and distance gates, Condorcet and Kemeny voting, a simulated-annealing ember bed, a Monte Carlo robustness court, a Pareto gate and more. A vending machine drops the verdict, a receipt prints, and a leave-one-out audit names the few stations that actually changed the answer, while a shadow run shows what simply taking the first idea would have chosen. Stations can be added, reordered and tuned, and the long game is a machine in which all forty visibly do something.
whyNow: Timeless: lunch recurs daily, and the punchline is measured by the page instead of asserted. It also fills this week's owed humor slot with a working tool rather than a one-liner.

research.summary: The overengineering joke is an established genre with a clear lineage: dictionaries define the Rube Goldberg sense as complex means for a simple end, and a long-running Java repository satirises enterprise software by piling layers onto FizzBuzz. Lunch deciders are a familiar startup exercise, so the gag alone is thin. The depth comes from methods that are real and checkable: Condorcet cycles, the Condorcet family used in Debian leader votes, simulated annealing (named for metallurgy, introduced 1983) and expected value of perfect information as the ceiling on what extra deliberation can buy. The research shapes the mechanic: every station reports a measured effect, a leave-one-out audit finds the load-bearing stations, and an EVPI-style closing stage delivers the annoyingly correct verdict, measured by the page rather than claimed, of how often the extra deliberation changed anything.

facts.claim: Merriam-Webster defines the adjective Rube Goldberg as accomplishing by complex means what seemingly could be done simply, and the Britannica dictionary gives the same sense: doing something simple in an unnecessarily complicated way.
Pairwise majority voting over three or more options can produce a cycle (A beats B, B beats C, C beats A) even when every voter's own ranking is consistent; this is the Condorcet paradox.
Simulated annealing takes its name from annealing in metallurgy (heating, then controlled cooling) and is credited to Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi in 1983.

The expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the most that removing all uncertainty before deciding could be worth; it is never negative and is an upper bound on the value of any other information gathering.
As of the 2024 and 2025 vote pages, the Debian project uses the Condorcet method for its leader elections, and a LinuxFr report describes Debian's variant as the Schulze method.

title: Group Chat Gremlin
pitch: Five friends choose a movie with a real Raft-style protocol: they elect a Planner, replicate everyone's ballots into a shared log, and decide once three ballots are committed. The visitor plays the network, holding, dropping or reordering messages and crashing one friend within a mischief budget, while ember timers go dark, elections split and the minutes of the meeting write themselves. research.summary: Prose analogies that cast Raft as friends choosing lunch or dinner are already common, and interactive Raft visualisations exist, so a passive explainer would be a repeat. The FLP result (1985) shows that with fully asynchronous delivery even one faulty process leaves every deterministic consensus protocol with a possible endless run, the Two Generals' Problem shows confirmations cannot remove doubt over lossy channels, and Raft answers with terms, majority votes and randomised election timeouts that make split votes unlikely, not impossible. Raft's five published safety properties give a live monitor that stays green whatever the visitor does, while ballot order decides which movie wins, which separates agreement from fairness. Lamport's Paxos paper was itself an allegory about a Greek parliament, which licenses the comic tone.

facts.claim: The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson result (Journal of the ACM, 1985) shows that every deterministic protocol for asynchronous consensus has a possible non-terminating run even if just one process may fail, because a crashed process looks the same as a slow one.

In Raft a follower that hears no heartbeat within a randomised timeout (150-300 ms is the commonly cited example) becomes a candidate for a new term; a majority of votes wins, each term has at most one leader, and a split vote simply triggers another round.
The Raft paper lists five safety properties that hold at all times: Election Safety, Leader Append-Only, Log Matching, Leader Completeness and State Machine Safety.
Over a channel that can lose messages, no finite exchange of confirmations lets two parties be certain they agree (the Two Generals' Problem); extra messages only move the doubt to the last one.
Lamport's Paxos paper, The Part-Time Parliament, frames the protocol as the legislators of an ancient Greek island and appeared in ACM Transactions on Computer Systems in 1998.

Casting Raft as friends choosing dinner or lunch is already an established explainer genre (a DEV Community post, a database vendor's film-themed blog post, a conference talk on what to eat for lunch), so the new angle is making the visitor the adversary instead of the spectator.

title: Moon Ferry
pitch: A visitor skippers a slow ferry across an invented strait where the tidal stream outruns the engine. They scrub an hour-by-hour stream atlas, read the day's tide table, pick a departure time and drag waypoints, and the boat then sails the plan while the arrows swing round and a shoal ledge dries and floods. Afterwards a solver reveals the fastest possible passage as a ghost boat and paints arrival-time isochrones that lean with the stream, so the visitor sees which minutes the moon took.
whyNow: October is king-tide season: station tables list a new-moon spring-tide window on Oct 10-11, 2026 and a larger perigean peak around Oct 26-28, so the autumn's strongest streams are due. The daily passage reads the real moon age, and the idea stays good all year because every coast keeps a tide table.

research.summary: Tidal navigation is a map that changes with the clock. Stream atlases print one chartlet per hour relative to high water at a standard port, with arrows whose paired numbers give neap and spring knots, and sailors turn tide tables into water depth with the rule of twelfths (1:2:3:3:2:1 of the range per hour). Tides repeat about every 12 h 25 min, so a tide table slides roughly 50 minutes a day. Tidal causeways such as Holy Island publish daily crossing windows that slide with the tide, the same timetable puzzle in real life. Minimum-time steering through a drifting current is Zermelo's problem; one 2019 arXiv paper reports analytic solutions can be unstable in turbulent flow (single source, unconfirmed), so the build searches a time-dependent grid instead. Station tables put the 2026 king-tide windows at Oct 10-11 and about Oct 26-28. The strait, ports and tide station are invented; the physics is simplified and labelled so.

design.coreLoop: Each passage runs briefing, planning, sailing and review. The visitor studies the tide table, tide curve and stream atlas, picks a departure hour and up to five waypoints with an aim-off angle per leg, and sees a live prediction of the track update. sophisticationHooks: Tide model with a spring-neap beat: two lunar-solar constituents plus the real moon age set height, and stream strength follows the rate of change of height, so slack water lands near high and low water.

title: Orbital Knitwear
pitch: A visitor tunes a satellite's height, tilt and orbit shape and watches its ground track unspool across a wool-textured world map, each pass adding a ribbon of stitches wherever the camera swath reaches. Pattern cards set goals such as seeing latitudes the space station never reaches, repeating the same track every 16 days, keeping a steady local time of day, or lingering over the far north. A flat-versus-polar toggle shows how the projection decides which holes look big, while the score counts true surface area.
whyNow: Timeless: orbital geometry never goes stale. The knitting frame makes a nerdy subject cozy, and the projection toggle and daylight terminator put a map argument at the centre.

research.summary: A ground track is a map argument: one orbit is a sine wave on a flat map and a spiral seen from the pole. Research shapes the mechanic. Earth's bulge (J2) turns an orbit's plane, and at about 98 degrees and 600-700 km that turn matches the Sun's 0.9856 degrees per day, so a satellite keeps one local solar time; a two-body-plus-J2 calculation done here gives 97.79 degrees at 600 km and 98.19 degrees at 700 km, matching both sources. Landsat's 16-day cycle of 233 orbits is a literal knitting gauge: tracks about 172 km apart against a 185 km swath. The ISS inclination of 51.6 degrees fences its track and Earth's spin moves each pass about 23 degrees west. Scoring by true area matters: the band poleward of 60 degrees is a third of an equirectangular map but about 13 percent of the planet (computed here). The Molniya figures are single-sourced.

You raise the scope for a few seconds, swing it onto an unmanned target barge, turn the handwheel until the two images of its mast meet to read the range, then drop below and pencil the fix on the chart. Two fixes reveal the barge's course and speed, you slide the aim point along its track until the practice round and the barge arrive together, and a dye splash tells you how good you were.

design.coreLoop: Each drill sends one to three unmanned barges across a range at constant course and speed. You raise the scope (a spray timer limits each look), find a barge in low power, switch to high power, name its class from the recognition book and turn the handwheel until the stacked images meet to read range. You lower the scope and the fix is pencilled on the chart with bearing and clock time. You wait, look again, and the two marks give a track with an uncertainty wedge. You drag the aim point along the track until the practice round and the barge arrive together, then fire; the dye splash scores the miss distance, with bonuses for fewer looks and less exposure. Every extra look is a value-of-information bet: minute two is learning the handwheel, minute ten is choosing the gap between looks.
sophisticationHooks: Real optics: a stacked-image handwheel (two copies of the target, offset until the mast tip meets the waterline) turns a known mast height into range. The player's alignment error and a mis-identified ship class both skew the fix, and low power finds targets while high power measures.

Estimation with honesty: two timed fixes give a velocity vector drawn with an uncertainty wedge that narrows as the gap between looks grows, so waiting longer buys accuracy at the price of a barge that may sail out of range.

Equal-arrival aiming: dragging the aim point along the predicted track races two phosphor timing bars (practice round against barge) and a lamp lights when they match. A final drill takes the stadimeter away so the player must move the boat to build a baseline, as bearings-only tracking requires.

Hero moment: the scope broaches and a brass-ringed lens rises through the waterline, spray beading and clearing, horizon swaying with the swell; when the dye lands it blooms across the hull while the green readout answers with a soft afterglow. Reduced motion swaps the sway and spray for fades.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: seeded sim core (kinematics, reading-error model, scoring), periscope canvas with low and high power and four invented ship silhouettes, recognition book, stacked-image handwheel, SVG chart table with pencil fixes and uncertainty wedge, equal-arrival aiming with two timing bars, six drills ending in a graduation certificate, URL-hash seeds, instructor lines, muted-by-default WebAudio, reduced-motion twin, keyboard and touch controls, about panel with sources. Cut first: the bearings-only final drill, then swell-hidden waterlines. Not built: night, weather, other weapons, leaderboards, any backend.
risks: Hook is single-sourced and inconsistent: the page will show 'Systems Offline' as reported on a jam page, as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io, and the Ludum Dare 60 dates as per its official page; the game works without either.

design.coreLoop: Wave loop: you read two patch notes, pick one with 1 or 2 (or a tap), watch the system-lamp board change as its true effect applies, then play a 30 to 40 second brick-breaker wave under every rule accumulated so far. Clearing the wave or losing a ball ends the loop with a 'known issues' reveal that tells you what the euphemism really meant and files it in the codex. Notes follow a learnable grammar (improved means faster with a catch, rebalanced means nerfed, deprecated means removed with compensation, reimagined means shuffled), so minute two is decoding and minute ten is routing synergies, such as a sticky paddle with gravity, around your build's weak spots. Ten waves end in a v1.0 launch card; three rollbacks end the run early. The daily seed makes the offers identical for everyone.
sophisticationHooks: A decodable grammar: eight verbs (improved, rebalanced, streamlined, reimagined, modernized, deprecated, added in beta, fixed) act on eight game systems (ball, paddle, ceiling, bricks, gravity, input, audio, juice), so a euphemism means the same kind of change everywhere. A codex fills in as you learn, which is what separates minute two from minute ten.

Generic modifier engine with synergy and clamps: about 40 valid verb-noun pairs stack, such as a sticky paddle with gravity or multiball with the ceiling deprecated, while a stall watchdog ships an in-fiction hotfix if no brick falls for 25 seconds.

The juice ladder: feedback layers (hit-stop, squash and stretch, trails, particles, shake, synthesized sound) arrive as patches, so the page shows game feel being built from silent grey boxes at v0.1 to a bright, noisy v1.0. Each layer has a reduced-motion twin and a shake toggle.

Hero moment: a board of system lamps clicks off or on when a patch lands, an installing-update wipe sweeps the playfield, and the same bricks that were flat grey rectangles burst into confetti by v1.0 while the changelog scrolls alongside.

title: Sound Lantern
pitch: A lantern that shines sound: a beam sweeps around the player like a lighthouse while walls hum and every passage mouth rings a chime whose pitch tells how deep it runs, and one input (space, tap, gamepad button or an assistive switch) commits to the passage the beam is crossing. Each sweep is a small gamble, because another full revolution gives better information while the flood rises, and the whole cave plays with the screen dark, or by radar and captions alone for players who cannot hear. Afterwards the cave is revealed as a map with the player's ribbon route beside the best route.
whyNow: Timeless as a design, with a seasonal nudge: October 15 is White Cane Safety Day in the US (as of 2026-10-11, per Paths to Literacy and Mass.gov). The page is framed as an audio game made for everyone, not as a simulation of blindness.

research.summary: Click echolocation is documented by independent research groups (blind experts, and sighted novices after training), so reading a space by ear is a real skill. Audio-only games with binaural 3D sound exist (an audio-only iPhone title; student and thesis projects for visually impaired players) and sighted players enjoy them too. Switch scanning, where an indicator advances on its own and one switch selects, is the standard single-input method in assistive technology, and the Game Accessibility Guidelines favor very simple control schemes for switch users. The precedence effect fuses echoes within a few to tens of ms, so the page codes distance by pitch and chimes instead of tiny delays. The secretary problem (the 37 percent rule) frames the sweep dilemma. Critiques from blind advocates of blindfold-style simulations shape the framing: an audio game, not a simulation.

facts.claim: Several independent research groups report that people, blind experts and sighted novices after training, can judge distance or position from the echoes of their own mouth clicks (PLOS ONE and PLOS Computational Biology papers seen in search results).

Audio-first games built on binaural or 3D directional sound exist: Papa Sangre is an audio-only iPhone game whose levels are navigated by sound alone, and academic projects (Connecticut College, UMass Dartmouth) built audio games for visually impaired players.
Switch access scanning advances an indicator through items on its own, by highlight or by voice, and the user selects the current item by activating a single switch.

As of 2026-10-11, per the Game Accessibility Guidelines, a guideline recommends very simple control schemes compatible with switch or eye-tracking devices, with a one-button endless runner as the example (reported by one organization, unverified).

In the precedence effect, similar sounds close together in time are heard as one event; the fusion window is roughly 1 to 5 ms for clicks and tens of ms (about 30 to 50) for complex sounds, beyond which a separate echo is heard.
In the secretary problem, rejecting roughly the first n/e (about 37 percent) of candidates and then taking the first one better than all seen so far succeeds with probability near 1/e.

design.coreLoop: At each chamber a beam of sound orbits the player once every few seconds (adjustable). A tick marks straight ahead, a continuous hum carries wall distance (nearer is brighter and louder), and each passage mouth rings a chime whose pitch encodes how far the passage runs, with wind layered on the exit direction and flutter on hazards. A single input commits to the passage under the beam at that instant (nearest mouth wins within an adjustable tolerance); a press between mouths bonks and costs a revolution. The player then walks the passage by footstep sound to the next chamber. A flood clock rises with every revolution, so each sweep poses an optimal-stopping choice between committing on partial information and paying for another full revolution. The run ends at the exit with a reveal map: the cave, the player's ribbon route, and the solver's best route. Daily seeds and hash-shared cave...
sophisticationHooks: One deterministic percept stream, four renderers: a pure core turns each sweep into timed events (hum curve, tick, chimes, wind, flutter), consumed by a WebAudio renderer (AudioParam value curves and scheduled oscillators on the audio clock), a canvas radar, an aria-live caption feed, and optional vibration, so hearing, sight and touch are equal ways to play.

Cave engine: seeded Poisson-disc chambers, a minimum spanning tree plus extra loops under a planarity check, zigzag passage ribbons, a union signed-distance field, 96 to 128 ray-marched samples per sweep with hysteresis opening detection, and Dijkstra over walking time plus sweeps for par; decoy alcoves are placed so a greedy deepest-chime policy sometimes fails.

Input timing core: the beam angle is a pure function of audio-clock time; a press maps through a latency offset from tap-along calibration, then through assist tolerance and snap-to-nearest-mouth, with revolution period and tolerance adjustable so players with slower or less precise input run at their own pace.

Hearing-robust coding: direction rides on stereo pan, on time since the tick, and on the chime pitch contour at once, so mono speakers, one-ear listening and different hearing profiles still work; a setup step sets the volume ceiling and pitch range behind a limiter.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: cave generator and solver (about 350 lines), sweep sampler and percept events (about 250), WebAudio renderer with six voices (hum, tick, chime, wind, flutter or drip, footstep) (about 300), canvas radar and reveal map (about 250), UI shell with settings (speed, tolerance, mono, captions, contrast, reduced motion, lights-out), about and making-of panel, daily seed with URL-hash sharing, localStorage bests. Cut if short: collectible moths, moving bats, biome variety, free-steer mode, spoken direction labels, vibration.
risks: Builders and QA cannot hear the result; mitigation: every mapping is a pure function with checkable outputs, captions mirror each percept in the DOM for inspection, and a built-in audio test strip plays each voice.
Disability-simulation critique (blind advocates, design writers): the copy presents an audio game for everyone and makes no empathy or blindfold claims; the about panel credits audio-game precedents.

Autoplay and mobile audio quirks: sound starts only after a gesture, resumes after tab changes, and the game pauses when hidden. Timing jitter and output latency vary by device; audio-clock timing plus calibration handle it, but headless QA cannot test it.
Loudness and hearing safety: a compressor, a volume ceiling and a setup step come before any sound plays.
Distance is coded by pitch and chimes, not realistic echo delays, because the precedence effect fuses short delays; the about panel says the acoustics are stylized.

title: Eyes Only
pitch: Each plate is a mosaic of colored dots hiding a creature or a letter, and each of five simulated eyes (typical, protan, deutan, tritan, achromat) reads a different part of the picture. The visitor flips lenses, with a severity dial for milder forms, to see what each eye reveals, decodes cipher words whose letters need different eyes, and builds plates in a studio where a solver tunes the dots until exactly the chosen eyes can read them. A real lab result, dichromats out-spotting trichromats on color-camouflaged texture, inspires the masked plates, so the eye most often called deficient is the one that cracks the code.

research.summary: A 1992 study reported that dichromats beat trichromats at finding texture-defined targets hidden by random red-green coloring, and a later review states dichromats do better when color is irrelevant to the task; early stimuli were stylized, so the effect is real but task-dependent. design.coreLoop: A seeded plate packs about two thousand dots of mixed radii; a hidden figure is encoded as a small offset in chosen cone-contrast directions (L, M, S or luminance) with masking noise in others. The visitor switches among five lenses (keys 1 to 5) or drags a severity dial, moves a reticle to the figure, and receives a per-lens detectability readout plus a reveal card explaining which eyes could read the plate and why. Cipher mode spreads a word over plates, one letter per subset of eyes. Studio mode takes a target set of readers and runs a solver that tunes channel amplitudes and noise until the model's detectability meets the target, or reports the target infeasible. A map of all 32 reader subsets fills in as plates are made, with unreachable cells greyed out, which gives a collection goal for the tenth minute.
sophisticationHooks: Lens engine: 3x3 linear-RGB simulation matrices in the Machado style with a severity dial from typical to full dichromacy (anomalous trichromacy included), an achromat luminance lens, and self-tests (neutral gray unchanged; red-green pairs collapse under deutan and protan; blue-yellow pairs collapse under tritan).

Plate generator: seeded blue-noise circle packing with mixed radii on a spatial hash grid, figure masks from signed-distance creature shapes and a 5x7 glyph set, dot colors sampled in a cone-contrast space with gamut-safe scaling, fully deterministic from the URL hash.

Detectability model: a d-prime style score per lens (figure versus ground difference over pooled noise in the channels the lens still has) plus a clutter term where chromatic noise masks luminance signals for lenses that still see it, the Morgan-style effect; exact plates (pure channel signals) are separated from perceptual plates (masking) and labeled.

Studio solver and feasibility map: coordinate-descent search with restarts over signal mix, amplitude and per-channel noise to hit any of the 32 reader subsets; subsets that violate the channel structure are shown infeasible under the model and greyed in the map.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: lens engine and self-tests (about 250 lines), generator and renderer (about 300), detectability model and solver (about 250), UI for Hunt, Cipher and Studio modes with keyboard reticle and touch, severity dial, reveal cards, 12 specimen shapes and the glyph set, 40 curated seeds, URL-hash sharing, about and making-of panel listing verified sources only. Cut if short: sonified plate (pitch from local detectability), image import, palette tool, per-lens custom mixing.
risks: Perceptual claims: whether a typical eye misses a masked plate depends on the person and the display; the page grades by the model and labels those plates perceptual, while exact plates are true by construction.
The page is a puzzle and a model, not a vision test or diagnosis; the copy avoids telling any visitor what their own vision is.

Simulation caveats: disability-simulation critiques, residual red-green discrimination reported for some dichromats (one source, unverified), and varied displays; the about panel states them and shows the residual-discrimination point as 'as of 2026-10-11, per UC eScholarship'.

The camouflage advantage is documented for stylized stimuli and specific tasks (per a review in the search results), so the copy states it as a lab result and makes no general claim about colorblind people.
Matrix constants have to be reproduced from the published model without opening it; the fallback derives lenses from an LMS projection and the self-tests check neutrals and confusion-pair collapse.
A visual puzzle is not fully playable by blind visitors; text reveal cards and the optional sonified plate (cut if short) are the mitigation.

title: Siege Of The Sink
pitch: Each night a seeded heap of dirty dishes besieges the kitchen, and the only fortress is a dishwasher drawn as a cross-section with two racks, a cutlery basket and a rotating spray arm. title: Second Pick Wins
pitch: A visitor picks a three-flip coin pattern, a smug bot picks its own after seeing it, and a flip-by-flip race decides whose pattern shows up first. Every first pick loses at least two thirds of the time to the best reply, so the visitor runs ten million simulated races and watches the bot's edge settle on exact fractions such as 2 to 1. Then the visitor takes the second pick and the table flips; a red-and-black card mode with tricks shows the same effect in a real deck.
whyNow: Timeless. The game is fair in each pick yet decided by the order of choosing, which makes it a durable argument-loser.

research.summary: In Penney's game two players each pick a short heads-tails pattern and the one that appears first in a fair coin sequence wins. Because picking is sequential, the second picker can answer any three-flip pattern with a reply that is strictly more likely to appear first (at least 2 to 1 for length 3, computed here from the leading-number formula). A short rule builds the reply, and Conway's leading-number method gives exact odds. A red/black card version with tricks (Humble-Nishiyama) exists. The page can show the payoff matrix for lengths 3 to 5, exact odds next to a seeded Monte Carlo, and expected waiting times. At length 3 the winning reply never has a longer average wait than the pattern it beats, but at length 4 it can (THTH, wait 20, beats HTHH, wait 18, with probability 9/14), which is where the loss feels unfair.
